In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of aquaporins, a family of membrane proteins that facilitate the movement of water across biological membranes.
the phosphorylation of the vasopressive regulated water channel, aquporin-2 (AQ2), and its regulation by AVP.
the regulation of Aqp2 phosphorylation at serine 256 and serine 261.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
vasopressin regulates AQP2 phosphorylation at serine 265 by phosphoproteome, and this phosphorylation regulates the water channel activity of AQP2.
vasopressin regulates aquaporin- 2 phosphorylation at serine 256 (pS256–AQP2), and this phosphorylation regulates AQP2 trafficking.
pS264 is an AVP-regulated phosphorylation site that is associated with AQP2-containing intracellular vesicles and the apical membrane, and that it is involved in AQP2 recycling.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the pS264–AQ2 phosphorylation site is a major site in the vasopressine-induced phosphorylation of AQP2, which is involved in the trafficking of the protein from intracellular vesicles to the apical plasma membrane of renal collecting duct cells.

the phosphorylation of S264 in AQP2 is a marker of AVP action and that it is a dynamic process, with AVP increasing pS264– AQP2 abundance and redistributing it from the intracellular vesicles to both the baso lateral and apical plasma membrane, and to the endosomal pathway.

the phosphorylation of AQP2 at S-264 is an early response to vasopressin and that this response is required for the vasopressine-dependent trafficking of the protein to apical membranes of collecting duct principal cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that

vasopressin increases the abundance of AQP2, and the phosphorylation of AQP2 at Ser-264 in the collecting duct, and that pS264– AQP2 is present in vesicles that are associated with the plasma membranes and endosomal compartments.
